title: Fixed-Width Types, Operators & Formatted Standard IO
summary: Master stdint.h fixed-width integer types, IEEE 754 floating point arithmetic, bitwise operators, and secure formatted IO with printf and fgets.
learningObjectives: Utilize portable fixed-width integers from <stdint.h> (uint32_t, int64_t)
Perform bitwise manipulation (AND, OR, XOR, shifts) for bitmasking
Avoid buffer overflows by replacing gets/scanf with fgets and snprintf
prerequisiteConcepts: Completion of Lesson 1: The C Compilation Pipeline

sections.heading: 1. Portable Integer Widths and Defensive Buffer IO
sections.content:
In traditional C, the size of `int`, `long`, and `short` is implementation-defined. An `int` may be 16 bits on an AVR microcontroller and 32 bits on x86_64, while `long` is 32 bits on 64-bit Windows but 64 bits on 64-bit Linux!

To write portable, bug-free systems software, C99 introduced `<stdint.h>`:
- `int8_t`, `uint8_t`: Exactly 8 bits.
- `int16_t`, `uint16_t`: Exactly 16 bits.
- `int32_t`, `uint32_t`: Exactly 32 bits.
- `int64_t`, `uint64_t`: Exactly 64 bits.
- `size_t`: Unsigned integer type representing object sizes and array indices.

Furthermore, reading user input securely requires avoiding deprecated functions like `gets()` (which has no buffer size limit) and unchecked `scanf("%s")`. Instead, always use `fgets()` with an explicit buffer limit.

codeExamples.code:
INTEGER BITMASKING BLUEPRINT:
Initial Byte:      [0][0][1][0] [1][0][1][0]  (0x2A)
Bitmask (Bit 3):   [0][0][0][0] [1][0][0][0]  (1 << 3)
---------------------------------------------
Bitwise AND (&):   [0][0][0][0] [1][0][0][0]  (Non-zero -> Bit 3 is SET)
Bitwise OR  (|):   Sets bit 3 high
Bitwise NOT (~):   Inverts all bits for clear operations: value &= ~(1 << 3)
codeExamples.explanation: Bitmask operations for querying, setting, and clearing individual hardware registers and permission flags.

keyPoints: Always prefer <stdint.h> fixed-width types over raw primitive types for cross-platform reliability.
Use fgets() rather than scanf() or gets() to eliminate buffer overflow attack vectors.
Print size_t with %zu and uint64_t with PRIu64 from <inttypes.h>.
commonMistakes: Using gets() which is vulnerable to catastrophic buffer overflows.
Assuming sizeof(long) is always 8 bytes across all 64-bit operating systems.

sections.heading: 2. Production Bitmask Engine and Defensive Input Parsing
sections.content: This program showcases bitmask state flags for network connections and parses user configuration defensively without buffer overflows.

codeExamples.explanation: Demonstrates bitwise flags manipulation with |= and &= ~, combined with bounds-checked snprintf formatting.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
State after connection & TLS handshake:
Connection Flags: 0x03
 - Connected:     YES
 - Encrypted:     YES
 - Authenticated: NO
 - Compressed:    NO

State after SASL authentication:
Connection Flags: 0x07
 - Connected:     YES
 - Encrypted:     YES
 - Authenticated: YES
 - Compressed:    NO

State after TLS termination:
Connection Flags: 0x05
 - Connected:     YES
 - Encrypted:     NO
 - Authenticated: YES
 - Compressed:    NO

Formatted Safe Session ID: SESSION-ID-1024

keyPoints: Use snprintf with sizeof(buffer) to safely prevent format string overflows.
Bitwise operations allow tracking up to 8 binary states in a single uint8_t byte.
commonMistakes: Using sprintf instead of snprintf, risking stack smashing on unexpected input sizes.

sections.heading: 3. Systems Architecture Blueprint & Production Verification
sections.content:
Mastering Fixed-Width Types, Operators & Formatted Standard IO requires continuous empirical verification. In production environments, verify that every memory allocation is accounted for, buffer boundaries are strictly honored, and execution logs provide deterministic diagnostics.

Key Operational Checks:
1. Validate inputs and boundary constraints before executing core business logic.
2. Structure error handling so failed operations release all acquired resources before returning.
3. Establish automated unit and regression tests that exercise edge conditions and stress boundaries.
keyPoints: Reliability in systems engineering is achieved by treating failure modes as first-class architectural concerns.
Document and verify performance invariants with repeatable benchmarks.
commonMistakes: Failing to profile and test under simulated peak load conditions.

exercises.title: Implement a Bitfield Permission System
exercises.objective: Create a permission validator that tests READ, WRITE, and EXECUTE bitmasks.
exercises.description: Write a function has_permission(uint8_t user_perms, uint8_t required_perms) that returns true only if all required bits are active.
instructions: Write boolean evaluation logic using bitwise AND.
Verify with test cases in main().
hints: An expression (user_perms & required_perms) == required_perms tests if all required bits are present.
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: Checking (user_perms & required_perms) == required_perms ensures every bit required by the mask is present.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: What format specifier must be used in standard C to print a size_t variable?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: %zu is the ISO standard format specifier for size_t integers.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: How do you clear (turn OFF) bit 2 in an integer variable 'flags'?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Bitwise AND with the bitwise NOT (~(1 << 2)) clears only the targeted bit while preserving all other bits.

recap: Fixed-width integer types from <stdint.h> provide guaranteed memory footprints. Bitwise operators enable compact flag tracking, and snprintf guarantees buffer safety.
